title: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO HAVE TWO WIVES—AND THE TERRIFYING WORDS HE SPOKE AFTERWARD
paragraphs: THE FIRST MAN IN THE BIBLE TO HAVE TWO WIVES—AND THE TERRIFYING WORDS HE SPOKE AFTERWARD

Before the flood, before the kings of Israel, and long before David and Solomon, one man took two wives. But the most disturbing part of his story isn't how many women he married. It's what happened to his heart—and how his story reveals humanity's desperate need for Jesus Christ.
There is a man in the Bible whose name most Christians have heard but whose story many have never truly examined.
He was not a king.
He was not a prophet.
He was not remembered for building an altar to God.
Yet in just a handful of verses, his life reveals something frightening about the human heart.
He had two wives.
He became the father of children whose contributions would help shape human civilization.
And then, one day, he spoke words so chilling that they exposed how far a human heart could drift from God while still living in a world full of remarkable achievements.
His name was Lamech.
And what makes his story unsettling is not merely that he was the first man explicitly recorded in Scripture as having two wives.
It's that his story appears in the same chapter where the Bible first tells us about murder.
Read that again.
The first recorded murder.
The first recorded polygamous marriage.
And a man who would eventually boast about taking a life.
All within the fourth chapter of Genesis.
Coincidence?
Scripture does not tell us that Lamech's marriages caused his violence. But the placement of these events invites us to look carefully at the world developing outside Eden.
Because sometimes the most frightening thing about sin is not how suddenly it destroys a person.
It's how gradually a person can become comfortable living with it.
And before we judge Lamech too quickly, there is something in his story that every one of us needs to confront.
Something that might be closer to home than we want to admit.
Genesis 4:19 records:
"And Lamech took unto him two wives: the name of the one was Adah, and the name of the other Zillah." — Genesis 4:19, KJV
There it is.
One sentence.
Two women.
One man.
A moment that marks the Bible's first explicit record of a man having multiple wives.
But the original Hebrew makes this account even more interesting.
The verse begins:
וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים
Vayyiqqaḥ-lo Lemeḵ shtei nashim.
Literally, the phrase communicates:
"And Lamech took for himself two wives."
The Hebrew expression shtei nashim means "two women" or "two wives," with the marital context making "wives" the appropriate translation.
And the phrase vayyiqqaḥ-lo, "he took for himself," describes Lamech's action. The wording alone does not prove his motives were selfish, abusive, or lustful.
That distinction matters.
We must never force Scripture to say more than God has revealed.
Yet the contrast with the creation account is difficult to overlook.
In Genesis 2:24, before sin entered the world, Scripture declared:
"Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh."
In Hebrew, the closing words are:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Vehayu levasar echad.
"And they shall become one flesh."
One flesh.
A covenant union.
A relationship established in God's good creation before shame, blame, jealousy, and violence entered human experience.
Jesus Himself later returned to this passage when teaching about marriage.
In Matthew 19:4–6, He appealed to God's creation of male and female and the two becoming one flesh, emphasizing the permanence and sacredness of the marriage bond.
So when Genesis 4 introduces Lamech with two wives, we are encountering the first recorded departure from the one-man, one-woman marriage pattern presented in Eden.
But we must be careful here.
The Bible does not say that Lamech was the first man in all human history to practice polygamy. It identifies him as the first person whose multiple marriages are explicitly recorded.
Nor does Genesis 4:19 pause to issue a direct command about his marriages.
It simply tells us what happened.
And that raises a question every serious Bible reader must learn to ask:
When Scripture records someone's behavior, does that automatically mean God approves of it?
Of course not.
The Bible records adultery, deception, murder, idolatry, betrayal, and countless other human failures.
Not because God celebrates them.
But because the Bible tells the truth about humanity.
Even when that truth is uncomfortable.
Even when the people involved are important.
Even when their lives contain remarkable achievements.
And Lamech's household was remarkable.
His first wife, Adah, gave birth to Jabal and Jubal.
Genesis 4:20 describes Jabal as the father of those who dwell in tents and keep livestock.
Genesis 4:21 identifies Jubal as the father of those who play the lyre and pipe.
His second wife, Zillah, gave birth to Tubal-cain, who worked with bronze and iron. The passage also names Tubal-cain's sister, Naamah.
Think about that.
Animal husbandry.
Music.
Metalworking.
Skills that would become deeply connected with human society and culture.
These were not insignificant people.
Their family was associated with developments that mattered.
And here is where the story becomes painfully relevant.
A person can contribute something valuable to the world and still have a heart that desperately needs God.
You can be gifted and spiritually lost.
Successful and inwardly empty.
Admired and privately cruel.
Talented enough to build something extraordinary while neglecting the condition of your own soul.
You can have a beautiful house and a broken marriage.
A growing business and a shrinking prayer life.
A respected name and a conscience you keep trying to silence.
You can even be deeply involved in Christian activities while quietly resisting the very Lord whose name you speak.
Not every outward success is evidence of God's approval of everything happening behind the scenes.
And not every outward struggle means God has abandoned someone.
The human heart is more complicated than appearances.
Maybe that is why Lamech's story is so unsettling.
His household was connected with remarkable human abilities.
But when the Bible finally lets us hear Lamech speak, we do not hear a prayer.
We do not hear gratitude.
We do not hear repentance.
We hear a song about violence.
And suddenly the atmosphere changes.
Genesis 4:23 says:
"And Lamech said unto his wives, Adah and Zillah, Hear my voice; ye wives of Lamech, hearken unto my speech: for I have slain a man to my wounding, and a young man to my hurt." — KJV
Imagine the scene.
Adah and Zillah are listening.
The man who shares their household demands their attention.
But instead of words of affection, humility, or confession, he announces that he has killed someone.
The Hebrew text reads:
כִּי אִישׁ הָרַגְתִּי לְפִצְעִי וְיֶלֶד לְחַבֻּרָתִי
Ki ish haragti lefitsi, veyeled lechabburati.
A close rendering is:
"For I have killed a man for wounding me, and a young man for striking me."

The precise circumstances remain uncertain. The parallel lines may describe one killing poetically rather than two separate victims. The text does not give us enough information to reconstruct the incident or determine every detail of Lamech's responsibility.
But the tone of his declaration is unmistakably alarming.
There is no recorded appeal for God's mercy.
No recorded confession of guilt.
No expression of sorrow for the dead.
Instead, the speech moves toward an extraordinary claim.
Genesis 4:24:
"If Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, truly Lamech seventy and sevenfold."
Seventy-sevenfold.
Consider the arrogance of that declaration.
Earlier in Genesis 4, Cain murdered his brother Abel.
When God confronted Cain, the consequences were severe.
Cain feared that someone would kill him, and God placed a protective sign upon him, warning against vengeance.
That protection was not a divine celebration of Cain's crime.
It was God's restraint upon further bloodshed.
But now Lamech invokes Cain's protection and declares an even greater measure of vengeance for himself.
The text does not record God granting Lamech that claim.
It is Lamech speaking.
And the difference matters enormously.
Cain feared being killed. Lamech spoke as though vengeance itself were his security.
One man trembled under the consequences of sin.
Another proclaimed his own terrible measure of retaliation.
And somewhere between those two generations, we see how violence can become something a person not only commits but also defends and celebrates.
That is a warning worth hearing.
Because sin does not always begin with someone proudly announcing rebellion against God.
Sometimes it begins with a small compromise.
A bitterness we refuse to surrender.
A secret we justify.
A boundary we keep moving.
A relationship we know is wrong but refuse to release.
A lie we repeat so often that eventually it feels like the truth.
At first, our conscience protests.
Then we explain ourselves.
Then we become defensive.
Then, if we continue resisting correction, we may begin defending the very thing that once troubled us.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment is not when we fall.
It is when we no longer believe we need to repent.
Have you ever been there?
Not necessarily in the dramatic sins of Lamech.
But in the quieter rebellion that hides behind ordinary routines?
You know you should forgive someone.
But you keep replaying the injury.
You know you should apologize.
But your pride insists they should apologize first.
You know something in your life needs to change.
But you have become skilled at explaining why it can wait.
You still believe in God.
You still know the language of faith.
You may even continue attending church.
But somewhere inside, surrender has been replaced with negotiation.
And the frightening thing is how normal it can begin to feel.
That is why Lamech's story cannot remain merely an ancient lesson about marriage.
It reaches into our homes.
Our private conversations.
Our wounded pride.
Our excuses.
Our relationships.
Our refusal to be corrected.
And it asks a question that is difficult to escape.
Are you allowing God's Word to change you, or are you trying to make God's Word excuse you?
There is another important truth we must not overlook.
Lamech's two wives were named Adah and Zillah.
They were real women within the biblical narrative, not merely symbols for a sermon.
Scripture does not tell us whether they willingly entered these marriages, how they felt about their circumstances, or what their daily relationships were like.
We should not invent their suffering, rivalry, or personal histories to make the account more dramatic.
But we can recognize that they lived in a household where a man openly spoke of killing and multiplied vengeance.
And that should make us think seriously about the people affected by our choices.
Because sin rarely stays as private as we imagine.
A father's unchecked anger can frighten an entire household.
A mother's unresolved bitterness can shape the atmosphere in which children grow.
A husband's dishonesty can wound his wife.
A wife's betrayal can devastate her husband.
A leader's pride can injure people who trusted him.
A believer's hypocrisy can discourage someone who was beginning to seek Christ.
Our decisions have consequences beyond ourselves.
And this is precisely why God's design for marriage must never be reduced to an argument about how many spouses someone may have.
Biblical marriage is about covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, truth, holiness, and responsibility before God.
It is not a license for domination.
It is not permission to mistreat someone in the name of spiritual authority.
It is not a competition for control.
And it is certainly not a place where cruelty should be excused by quoting Scripture.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
That is the opposite of selfish power.
Jesus did not love His bride by exploiting her.
He gave Himself for her.
He laid down His life.
He showed that godly love is measured not by how much control someone possesses but by how faithfully that person loves in obedience to God.
And this is where we must confront another difficult question.
If Lamech was the first recorded polygamist, why do later biblical figures such as Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon also have multiple wives?
Doesn't that mean God approved of polygamy?
Not necessarily.
We must distinguish between what God permits or tolerates within fallen human history and what He presents as His original design.
Genesis describes multiple marriages without treating every action of the patriarchs as exemplary.
Abraham's household experienced painful conflict involving Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob's family was marked by rivalry, favoritism, and deep relational wounds.
David's household suffered devastating consequences amid his many moral failures.
Solomon's many wives turned his heart toward other gods, as recorded in 1 Kings 11.
These accounts differ in their circumstances, and we should not claim that every family tragedy was caused solely by polygamy.
But neither should we turn the Bible's descriptions of these marriages into a blanket endorsement.
Deuteronomy 17:17 specifically warned Israel's future king against multiplying wives.
And when Jesus taught about marriage, He did not point to Solomon's household as the ideal.
He returned to Genesis.
To the beginning.
To God's design.
That is what makes biblical interpretation so important.
We cannot simply ask, "Did someone in the Bible do this?"
We must also ask, "What does the whole counsel of Scripture reveal about God's will?"
Because the Bible is not merely a collection of stories about people we should imitate.
It is the unfolding revelation of God's work in a world shattered by sin.
And ultimately, it leads us to Jesus.
But before we reach the beauty of grace, there is one more connection in Lamech's story that deserves our attention.
One that many readers miss.
Lamech declared vengeance seventy-sevenfold.
Centuries later, Jesus spoke about forgiveness using strikingly similar language.
In Matthew 18:21, Peter approached Jesus and asked how often he should forgive someone who sinned against him.
Would seven times be enough?
Jesus answered in Matthew 18:22:
"I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." — KJV
The Greek phrase is:
ἕως ἑβδομηκοντάκις ἑπτά
Heōs hebdomēkontakis hepta.
This expression can be understood as "seventy-seven times" or "seventy times seven," depending on how the construction is interpreted. The familiar King James rendering is "seventy times seven."
The Greek wording also echoes the numerical expression found in the Greek Old Testament's rendering of Genesis 4:24.
We should not claim with absolute certainty that Jesus was deliberately quoting Lamech.
Matthew does not explicitly say that.
But the contrast is profound.
Lamech's words magnified vengeance.
Jesus' words magnified forgiveness.
Lamech spoke of retaliation.
Jesus taught His disciples to forgive repeatedly.
Lamech's declaration displayed the human desire to answer injury with greater injury.
Jesus revealed a kingdom where mercy breaks the endless cycle of revenge.
Do you see the beauty?
Humanity had learned to multiply vengeance.
Jesus taught His followers to multiply forgiveness.
And He did not merely teach it.
He lived it.
When Jesus was crucified, He suffered mockery, injustice, humiliation, and unimaginable pain.
Yet Luke 23:34 records His prayer:
"Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do."
The One who had every right to judge was praying for mercy.
The sinless Son of God was giving His life for sinners.
And suddenly, the story of Lamech becomes part of something much larger.
Not because Lamech secretly represents Christ.
Not because Genesis 4 directly predicts the crucifixion.
But because the Bible's unfolding story reveals the depth of humanity's sin and the greatness of the Savior we need.
Lamech's world was marked by vengeance.
Our world still is.
Look around.
Families destroyed by pride.
Marriages wounded by betrayal.
Friendships abandoned over unforgiven offenses.
Churches divided by bitterness.
People who would rather win an argument than restore a relationship.
People who carry wounds for decades because nobody ever taught them how to surrender their pain to God.
And then Jesus enters the story of humanity.
Not as another violent man demanding revenge.
But as the righteous Savior who willingly bears the punishment of sin.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were still sinners.
Not after we cleaned up our lives.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we proved ourselves worthy.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That is grace.
But grace is not permission to remain in rebellion.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners also calls them to repentance.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the gospel."
Repent.
Believe.
Turn from sin and trust in Christ.
The Gospel does not tell us that our wrongdoing was harmless.
It tells us that our wrongdoing was so serious that we needed a Savior—and that God's love was so great that He gave His Son.
That is why we must never confuse forgiveness with pretending evil did not happen.
Forgiveness does not mean remaining in danger.
It does not require an abused person to return to an unsafe relationship.
It does not erase accountability or the need for justice.
Biblical forgiveness releases personal vengeance into God's hands while pursuing truth, wisdom, and righteousness.
And reconciliation, where possible, requires more than sentimental words.
It requires truth, repentance, and a rebuilding of trust.
Jesus never calls us to make peace with sin.
He calls us to surrender it.
Perhaps someone reading this is carrying a secret.
Something you have hidden for years.
A decision you regret.
A relationship you damaged.
A marriage you betrayed.
A child you failed.
A parent you dishonored.
A season of your life that still fills you with shame.
And you have wondered whether God could ever receive someone like you.
Listen carefully.
The Bible does not tell us whether Lamech ever repented.
We do not know how his earthly story ended.
We must not invent an ending Scripture never gives.
But we do know what the Gospel promises to sinners who turn to Jesus Christ.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
The forgiveness Christ offers is not earned by impressive religious performance.
It is received through faith in Him, the crucified and risen Lord.
And genuine faith does not leave us indifferent to sin.
God's grace begins transforming the heart.
That transformation may involve painful honesty.
Confession.
Apologies.
Restitution where appropriate.
Accountability.
Learning new patterns.
Walking away from what once controlled us.
And sometimes accepting that people we wounded will need time to heal.
Grace does not erase every earthly consequence.
But it does mean your past does not have to remain the master of your future.
Because Jesus Christ is not merely interested in making you feel better about who you used to be.
He is making His people new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
That is not a promise that every struggle disappears overnight.
It is a declaration of a new identity and a new life in Christ.
And perhaps that is the word someone needs tonight.
You have spent years defining yourself by your worst chapter.
The affair.
The addiction.
The anger.
The divorce.
The lies.
The years you wasted.
The people you disappointed.
The prayers you stopped praying.
You have been living as though the most shameful thing you ever did must become the final description of who you are.
But if you are in Christ, your identity is not ultimately determined by your worst sin.
It is determined by the Savior who redeemed you.
Your past may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have to become your god.
Your failures may require confession and consequences.
They do not place you beyond the reach of Christ's mercy.
And your brokenness does not disqualify you from coming to the One who came to save sinners.
Not because sin is small.
But because Christ is greater.
Not because every broken relationship will automatically be restored.
But because God can restore sinners to Himself and teach them to walk in truth.
Not because the past never happened.
But because the cross and resurrection of Jesus Christ have opened the way to forgiveness, redemption, and new life.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not as someone looking for a perfect religious answer.
But as someone who understands that we all need mercy.
What is one area of your life where you need Jesus to replace pride with surrender, bitterness with forgiveness, or hiding with honesty?
You do not have to expose private details or name anyone.
And if God has already brought you through a season of repentance, healing, or restoration, consider sharing a brief testimony.
Your words may remind another person that they are not the only one seeking God's mercy.
Sometimes the testimony someone needs to hear is not from a famous preacher.
Sometimes it is from an ordinary believer who can say:
"I was wrong. I needed Jesus. And by His grace, I am learning to walk differently."
Not as another piece of content to forget tomorrow.
For the moment pride tells you not to apologize.
For the night when shame whispers that God could never forgive you.
Return to the Scriptures.
Read Genesis 4.
Read Matthew 18.
Read Romans 5.
And remember that the God who exposes sin also calls sinners to receive His mercy through Jesus Christ.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider sharing this article with them.
Not to shame them.
Not to send a hidden accusation.
But because you genuinely care about their soul.

Whether they are mature believers, struggling Christians, people who have grown cold in faith, or seekers still asking questions about Jesus, there is room to begin a serious conversation about the truth of God's Word.
Because the goal is not merely to gather an audience.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, repent of sin, trust Christ, and grow in faithful discipleship.
And if this ministry has been helping you grow, there is another meaningful way to stand with the mission.
But it is important to understand something.
The New Testament teaches generous, willing, and cheerful giving—not financial pressure as a condition of spiritual acceptance.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
You do not have to pay to receive God's grace.
It can help us continue publishing biblical teaching, reaching more readers, and developing resources that encourage people to grow deeper in Christ.
Those products are not the heart of the mission.
They are simply another way to share encouragement and Scripture-centered messages in everyday life.
The heart of the mission remains Jesus Christ.
His Word.
His Gospel.
His transforming grace.
And the people who still need to hear about Him.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture, develop a deeper prayer life, strengthen their understanding of the Gospel, and grow in their walk with Jesus.
But if you want to go beyond reading and become a regular supporter of this ongoing work, we warmly invite you to join us.
Read.
Pray.
Invite others.
Encourage someone to open the Bible.
A sincere conversation about Christ can matter more than you realize.
Every believer has opportunities to serve the Lord, whether through giving, teaching, prayer, hospitality, encouragement, or faithful witness.
What matters is that we serve from love and obedience to Christ, not from guilt or the desire to earn His approval.
And now, before you leave, return with me to the beginning.
To a man named Lamech.
To two wives named Adah and Zillah.
To a household remembered for music, livestock, and metalworking.
To a voice that proclaimed vengeance instead of repentance.
And to a chapter of Scripture that shows how deeply human life had been affected by sin.
We cannot change what Lamech said.
We cannot rewrite his recorded actions.
We cannot pretend the violence of Genesis 4 never happened.
But we can listen to the warning.
We can examine our own hearts.
We can refuse to make peace with the sins that are destroying us.
And we can turn to Jesus Christ.
Because the final word over the repentant believer is not the arrogance of Lamech.
It is not the violence of Cain.
It is not the shame of Eden.
It is the saving work of Jesus Christ—the One who died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, just as the Scriptures proclaim in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
Lamech's song declared the multiplication of vengeance.
Christ's Gospel announces forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
And that leaves every one of us with a decision.
Will we continue defending the things God is calling us to surrender?
Or will we come to Christ with empty hands and an honest heart?
Maybe tonight is the night you stop hiding.
Maybe it is the night you finally confess what you have been justifying.
Maybe it is the night you ask forgiveness from someone you have wounded.
Maybe it is the night you open your Bible again after years of silence.
Maybe it is the night you stop believing that your worst chapter must become your final chapter.
If that is you, pray sincerely:

"Lord Jesus, I have sinned against You. I have defended things I should have confessed. I have carried pride, bitterness, and shame. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You in truth. Help me turn away from sin and trust Your grace. Amen."
And remember, the power is not in repeating a particular prayer.
Salvation is found in Jesus Christ, received by grace through faith.
If this is the beginning of your return to Him, tell a trusted, biblically grounded Christian who can pray with you and help you grow.
You do not have to pretend you have everything figured out.
But you do need to take seriously the One who calls you to follow Him.

The most tragic thing about Lamech's story is not that we remember his sin. It is that Scripture never tells us he laid down his pride—and you still have the opportunity to lay down yours at the feet of Jesus.
